alternative: Return real `boolean` values from named predicates (`isEmpty()`, `isValid()`) and compare explicitly (`=== true`, `!== null`) instead of relying on truthiness; normalize at boundaries with `Boolean(x)`/`!!x`, and keep booleans out of arithmetic (`true + 1 === 2`).
idiom_name: named predicate returning a primitive boolean
implementation_notes: Boolean coercion (ToBoolean) is not user-overridable: every object is truthy, `if (x)` never calls `valueOf` or `Symbol.toPrimitive`, and there is no type system to enforce a restricted conversion, so the classic safe-bool structure cannot exist - adding it is not merely discouraged by convention, it is impossible. The JavaScript-appropriate replacement is an explicit predicate returning a primitive boolean, tested as `if (q.isEmpty())`; `Boolean(x)`/`!!x` belong only at boundaries where a value must be normalized, and booleans must be kept out of arithmetic because `true + 1 === 2`.
pitfalls: Truthiness and `== false` disagree: `[]` is truthy yet `[] == false` is true, and `"0"` is truthy yet `"0" == false` is true - equality tests are not truth tests.
`new Boolean(false)` is an object and therefore truthy, and `Boolean(wrapper)` returns true; never wrap booleans, and never widen a `boolean` into `Boolean`.
`true + 1` is 2, `true * 'x'` is NaN and `if (count)` treats 0 as absent - every coercion the safe-bool idiom exists to block is available in the language.
